name: Sahro Osman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. The Danish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Thomas Winkler, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and their Co-Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen, from Ministry of Justice. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The applicant’s father returned to Denmark, he was summoned for an interview with the Immigration Service on 10 November 2003. An interview was conducted with the help of an English/Somali interpreter although it was stated that the applicant spoke Danish. The applicant explained that she had taken care of her grandmother, who had fallen seriously ill, until some of the grandmother's children had arrived from Somalia to take over the care of their mother. The Immigration Service found that the applicants residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. They also considered that she was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Alien Act, since the applicant was 17 years old. The applicant appealed against the decision and maintained that it had not been her decision to leave the country. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision of 21 December 2006. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. It was also stated that her sister had assisted her in answering the questionnaire. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. The application was made in July 2007 and it was upheld on 1 October 2007. The case was heard at the Immigration Court in Copenhagen, Denmark, on 14 October 2007, and the decision was returned to the Migration Service on 21 December 2007. The applicant's parents had custody over her at the time of her departure, and could thus lawfully make decisions about [her] personal circumstances. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark. On 25 April 2008 it found against the applicant. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children under 15 years instead of under 18 years. It was preferable for foreign minors living in Denmark to arrive as early as possible and spend as many of their formative years as possible in Denmark. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant's parents sent her voluntarily to Kenya to live with family for an indefinite period. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. By letter of 27 January 2010 the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien’s Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) on 19 July 2009. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8. The Danish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Thomas Winkler, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and their Co-Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen, from Ministry of Justice. The application was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant's father had been informed that he, who had been recognised as a refugee, had visited his country of origin. The Immigration Service found that the applicant’s residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. They also considered that she was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Amnesty Act, since the applicant was 17 years old. Finally, it found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permitunder section 9 c, section 9 (ii) of the Alien Act. The application was made on 21 December 2006. In April 2007 the applicant appealed against the decision and maintained that it had not been her decision to leave the country. In June 2007 she re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. In October 2007 the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs (Ministeriet for flygtninge, indvandrere og integration) upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December2006. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children under 15 years instead of under 18 years. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention as invoked by the applicant. The applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in Kenya. On 11 December 2007 the Immigration Service brought the case. before the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret), before which the case was decided on the documents submitted, without any parties being summoned. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. 30 October 2008 the High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. By letter of 27 January 2010 the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien's Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The application for asylum under section 7 of the Aliens Act will be made in due course. The case was brought by a 16-year-old girl who applied to re-enter Denmark in August 2005.

The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Somali national. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The application was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant’s father returned to Denmark in November 2003. The Immigration Service took the stand that his residence permit had not lapsed. In August 2005, three months before the applicant turned eighteen, she contacted the Danish Embassy in Nairobi with a view to returning to live with her mother and siblings in Denmark. On 21 December 2006, the Immigration Service found that the applicant's residence. permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens. Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. They also considered that she was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the. Aliens Act, in force at the relevant time, since the applicant was 17 years old. The applicant appealed against the decision and maintained that it had not been her decision to leave the country. In June 2007 she re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. An earlier version of this article stated that the applicant had not seen her mother for four years. We are happy to clarify that this was not the case and that the application was based on a questionnaire filled out by the applicant in July 2007. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg. Immigration Service brought the case concerning section 17 and section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act before the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret), before which the case was decided on the documents submitted. On 25 April 2008 it found against the applicant. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret), henceforth the applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in Kenya. On 11 December 2007 the applicant, who was represented by counsel, asked the immigration service to bring the case. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention as invoked by the applicant and that her parents could lawfully make decisions about her personal circumstances. The High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien's Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The case was heard at the Supreme Court (Højesteret) on 19 January 2008. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Supreme Court was refused on 19 February 2008. The High Court refused to review the final administrative decision of refusal of a residence permit under section 9c, subsection 1, of the Aliens Act.

name: Andrzej Makowski
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested in Blanes, Spain, under an international search and arrest warrant on suspicion of having committed several offences of fraud, forgery, perjury, uttering threats, robbery and kidnapping. On 28 April 2003 the applicant was brought to Poland. He was remanded in custody until 30 June 2003. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was decided on 29 May 2007 by the President of the Fourth Section of the Court. The applicant maintains that when he was detained between 28 April 2003 and 1 April 2004 he was subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment. The bill of indictment listed several charges of fraud, forgery, perjury, robbery and kidnapping brought against thirteen accused. The court found that the evidence obtained in the case sufficiently supported the charges laid against him. It referred to the likelihood of a severe sentence of imprisonment being imposed on the applicant. The applicant made an application for release. He requested that his detention be replaced by another preventive measure. His application was dismissed on 8 July 2005. The case was very complex and the trial court dealt promptly with the case. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Katowice Court of Appeal under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed on 27 September 2006. The proceedings are still pending. The court noted that the court, when deciding on administrative and procedural matters, acted without delay. It further considered irrelevant the fact that at the material time the trial had not yet commenced. It noted that there were no delays for which the Regional Court could be held responsible for which it could be blamed. The hearings scheduled for 21 April, 5 May and 19 May 2006 were adjourned. On 2 June 2006 the court held the first hearing on the merits. The case was referred to the Katowice Regional Court for consideration. The applicant withdrew his complaint on 5 May 2006 about the length of the proceedings before the District Court. On 17 May 2006 the Katewice Regional court discontinued the proceedings, since the applicant had withdrawn his complaint. The case was settled in a settlement of more than $1.5 million. The settlement was reached in May 2006 and the case was dismissed on 18 May 2006. The appeal was heard by the Supreme Court of Poland in May 2007. The application was settled on 21 May 2007 and the settlement was concluded on 26 May 2007, with both sides agreeing that the case should be settled in the High Court of Justice.

The court found that the evidence obtained in the case sufficiently supported the charges laid against him. The applicant requested that his detention be replaced by another preventive measure. The applicant's case was referred back to the Katowice District Court. The hearings scheduled for 21 April, 5 May and 19 May 2006 were adjourned. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed on 27 September 2006. The proceedings are still pending. The court held the first hearing on the merits on 2 June 2006 and ordered that the applicant be forbidden to leave his place of residence. The trial had not yet commenced at the time of the hearing. The applicant had withdrawn his complaint on 5 May 2006 about the length of the proceedings before the District Court. name: Mustafa Yalgın
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the complaint and declared the remainder of the case inadmissible. The case was decided in favour of the applicant. The decision was published in the journal ‘Human Rights’ (‘The Rights of the Person’). The author is a Turkish national, and the case was heard in the Court of Justice. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the Dev-Yol. In his questioning by the investigating judge he denied the allegations against him and submitted that the police officers took his statements under duress. The court sentenced the applicant under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. The case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) in 1995. The applicant was conditionally released pending trial in the Ankara Martial Law Court (sıkıyönetim mahkemesi) in 1991.

The judge in the case, Rıza Türmen, was the only member of the Government of Turkey to sit on the Court. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the Dev-Yol. The public prosecutor accused the applicant of having been involved in a number of crimes such as killings, attacks and bombings. His case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay). The applicant was conditionally released pending trial on 22 July 1991. On 27 December 1995 the Court ofCassation upheld the applicant’s conviction.

name: Eileen Appleby
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that they had been prevented from meeting in the town centre, a privately owned shopping mall, to impart information and ideas about proposed local development plans. The application was sent to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing on admissibility and the merits took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 15 October 2002. The Court heard addresses by Mr Crow and Mr Singh. By a decision of 12 November 2002, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The town centre of Washington (Tyne and Wear) was originally built by the Washington Development Corporation (‘the Corporation’) The freehold of the careers’ office and the public library was owned by the Council, the social services office and health centre were leased to the Council by the Secretary of State. There was a post office within the Galleries and also the offices of the housing department. In 1997 the Council gave outline planning permission to the City of Sunderland College to build on a part of Princess Anne Park in Washington known as the Arena. The first to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth applicant to campaign against the college’s proposal. The Galleries were used for a consultation exercise by Sunderland Council in 2001. In March 1998 applicants were allowed to set up stands in the Galleries to collect signatures for a further petition. However, the same permission was not granted in April 1998 when the applicants wanted to collect more signatures. The Galleries' manager said he was obliged to refuse permission for them to do so as the building works were still underway. The deadline for letters of representation to the Council regarding the building work was 1 May 1998. On 30 April 1998 the applicants submitted the 3,200 letters of representations they had obtained. The Council ran a consultation campaign under the banner ‘Your Council, Your Choice’. 8,500 people were reported as having responded to the survey. The Local Government Act 2000 required local authorities to draw up proposals for the operation of ‘executive arrangements’ and consult local electors before sending them to the Secretary of State. Some 8,500 were reported to have responded to a survey conducted by the Local Government Association. It said: ‘We are happy to confirm that we have received and responded to all of the questions put to us by the LGA.’ The LGA added: “We are pleased to have received the information and are looking forward to the next step in the process.”

The application was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that they had been prevented from meeting in the town centre, a privately owned shopping mall, to impart information and ideas about proposed local development plans. A hearing on admissibility and the merits took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 15 October 2002. The Court heard addresses by Mr Crow and Mr Singh. By a decision of 12 November 2002, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Government replied to the application. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court. Around September 1997 the Council gave outline planning permission to the City of Sunderland College to build on a part of Princess Anne Park in Washington. The first to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth group to campaign against the proposal. The applicants had to remove their stands and stop collecting signatures. The campaign was unsuccessful and the college was allowed to build the Arena, the only playing field in the area which is available for use by the local community. The application was brought to the Court of Appeal by a group calling themselves Washington First Forum. The Court ruled in favour of the group and the application was dismissed. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of England and Wales. In 1998 the third applicant, as acting chair of Washington First Forum, wrote to the manager of the Galleries asking for permission to set up a stand and to canvass views from the public. In his reply of 14 April 1998, the manager refused access. The fourth applicant continued to try and reach the public by setting up stands by the roadside on public footpaths and going to the old town centre at Concord which, however, is visited by a much smaller number of Washington residents. On 30 April 1998 the applicants submitted the 3,200 letters of representation they had obtained. This was a statutory consultation exercise carried out under section 25 of the Local Government Act 1983. From 31 January to 6 March 2001, Sunderland Council ran a consultation campaign under the banner ‘Your Council, Your Choice’ 8,500 people were reported as having responded to the survey. The Local Government Act 2000 required local authorities to draw up proposals for the operation of ‘executive arrangements’ and consult local electors before sending them to the Secretary of State. The proposals were to be put to local authorities for their approval. The survey was carried out on behalf of the Local Government Association (LGA) and the Council for Local Government (CLG) The LGA is a body which advises local authorities on issues relating to local government. The CLG was set up by the LGA to allow local councils to decide on issues such as budgets and spending. The LGC is made up of local authorities, which can decide how much money is spent.

The application was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that they had been prevented from meeting in the town centre, a privately owned shopping mall, to impart information and ideas about proposed local development plans. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court heard addresses by Mr Crow and Mr Singh. By a decision of 12 November 2002, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The case was heard by the Chamber of the European Court of Human rights in Strasbourg. The first, second and third applicants were born in 1952, 1966 and 1947 respectively and live in Washington (Tyne and Wear) The new town centre of Washington is known as ‘the Galleries’ and is located within an area now owned by Postel Properties Limited. In 1997 the Council gave outline planning permission to the City of Sunderland College to build on a part of Princess Anne Park in Washington known as the Arena. The first to third applicants, together with other concerned residents, formed the fourth applicant to campaign against the college’s proposal and to persuade the Council not to grant the college permission. The applicants had to remove their stands and stop collecting signatures. The Salvation Army, Royal British Legion and local school choirs were given permission to set up stands and displays in the Galleries. Sunderland Council ran a consultation campaign under the banner ‘Your Council, Your Choice’, informing the local residents of three leadership choices for the future of the Council. Proceedings Act, the court had to take the interests of the. child'sWell-being into account, despite the fact that the return. order was final. Court denied that there was any risk of psychological harm on account of the child's tender age. In these circumstances, it could not be excluded that the child, who was now more than two years old and had been living solely with her mother for more than a year, would suffer grave psychological harm in the event of a return to her father. The question whether the return order could be enforced by coercive measures needed further examination, including an opinion by an expert in child psychology. It might also prove necessary to assess whether or not the mother's allegations were at all true. The court read out the police statements that were taken from M.Ç., M.P. and A.Y. to the applicants and asked the latter to comment on them. They denied the content of these documents. They further stated that they had no idea as to how their names had appeared on the computer hard disks that were seized during the raid in Mardin.

The applicants gave statements to the police where they accepted the charges against them. They denied the content of their police statements alleging that they were taken under duress. On 27 December 2001 the Diyarbakır State Security Court noted that the applicants' police statements were supported by information gathered from the archive of the organisation and further evidence. It accordingly convicted the applicants of the offence as charged and sentenced them to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. The applicants appealed. The Court of Cassation, having regard, inter alia, to the opinion of the Principal Prosecutor, upheld the judgment of the Diedarbak Turkish State Security court.

train_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applications were introduced on 18 August and 10 December 1997 and were registered on 25 August and 19 December 1997 under file nos. 37475/97 and 39036/97, respectively. The applicants complained, under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, that they were denied a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The Commission gave notice of the applications to the respondent Government and invited them to submit their observations on their admissibility and merits. The Government, represented by Mr Martin Eaton, Agent, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, responded by letter dated 20 November 1998, stating that it did not have any observations to make. Both applicants were serving in the British Army at the time of the case. Mr Smith was found guilty of four disciplinary offences of conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline. He was sentenced to be dismissed from the army, although section 69 provides for a maximum sentence of two years’ imprisonment (see paragraph 17 below). Mr Ford was convicted of three counts of common assault contrary to Criminal Justice Act 1988 and sentenced to six months’ jail. The applicants’ subsequent petitions and appeals, as far as the full Courts-Martial Appeal Court, were unsuccessful. March 1999 the Chamber decided to join the cases and not to hold a hearing on the merits. The Chamber also declared the applications admissible.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The applicant complained that, in the proceedings for review of his pre-trial detention, the Court of Appeal had unlawfully deprived him of his liberty. He also claimed that his defence counsel had been refused access to the investigation files. On 27 October 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was suspected of having evaded turnover taxes of 57,374 euros (EUR) He had to be placed in pre-trial detention because of a danger of collusion (Verdunkelungsgefahr) The documents seized were incomplete. There was therefore a risk that the applicant, if released, might destroy the missing documents or conceal further business transactions and accounts. He argued that he had a right to inspect the files in order to examine all the facts and evidence on which the arrest warrant and the strong suspicion that an offence had been committed were based. The applicant argued that there was no risk of collusion or of his absconding. Mönchengladbach District Court upheld the arrest warrant on 16 August 2002. The Regional Court’s review of the detention order on 9 September 2002 dismissed the applicant's appeal against the District Court's decision. On 16 September 2002 the applicant, represented by counsel, lodged a further appeal against his detention order. The Court of Appeal has now upheld the Regional Court's detention order against the applicant. The applicant is now being held in custody until his next court appearance on 18 January 2015. He is accused of evading income, turnover and trade taxes and is facing a heavy sentence. He was also accused of conspiring to mislead the authorities about his true location. The applicant appealed the detention order issued by the District Court on 25 July 2002. He claimed that he had a constitutional right to be given access to the facts and evidence on which the order was based. The Düsseldorf Court of Appeal quashed the previous decisions of the Mönchengladbach Regional Court on 9 September 2002 and on 16 August 2002. The court found that the Detention Order did not comply with the legal requirements. The facts leading to a strong suspicion that the accused had committed a particular offence and the reasons for detention had to be established. The detention order was quashed on 14 October 2002 and the case was remitted to the District court. The Court of Appeal noted that, in its decisions on the applicant’s detention, the District Court had, however, merely stated that the applicant was strongly suspected of tax evasion. This defect had not been remedied in the course of the subsequent decisions. be set out in the detention order. As counsel for the defence had also been refused access to the case files under section 147 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, these defects amounted to a denial of the right of the accused to be heard. As a consequence, the applicant remained in custody. On 29 October 2002 the Mönchengladbach District Court heard representations from the applicant, his defence counsel, the Public Prosecutor’’ and an official in charge of investigations at the D. The applicant’s counsel complained that he had not been granted access to the case files before the hearing. The Mönchengladbach District Court then issued a fresh detention order against the applicant. It stated that there was a strong suspicion that the applicant had evaded taxes on some twenty occasions between 1991 and June 2002. He faced a lengthy prison sentence which could no longer be suspended on probation, had not notified the authorities of his place of residence for several years and had claimed that he was living in the Netherlands. The District Court suspended the execution of the order to release the applicant at the request of the Public Prosecutor's Office, which had immediately lodged an appeal. The applicant was released from prison on 7 November 2002. He lodged a complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court against the decision of the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal dated 14 October 2002 and the detention order issued by the Mönchengladbach District Court on 25 July 2002. In his submission, his rights to liberty, to be heard in court and to be informed promptly by a judge of the reasons for his detention on remand as well as his right to a fair trial had been violated. The applicant withdrew his further appeal against the Regional Court’s decision on 10 December 2002. The Public Prosecutor’S Office granted the applicant's counsel access to the case files. The applicant was convicted of eight counts of tax evasion and sentenced to a total of one year and eight months’ imprisonment suspended on probation. The court found that the applicant, who had confessed to the offences, had evaded turnover taxes of DEM 129,795, income taxes of Dem 344,802 and trade taxes ofDEM 55,165. The Court of Appeal’s refusal to quash the detention order and to take a decision itself and its decision to remit the case to the District Court instead had also breached his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. The Federal Constitutional Court, without giving further reasons, declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint against the detention orders.

name: Mehmet Güneş
train_texts: The case was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) on 23 July 2000. The applicant was born in 1951 and lives in Turkey. He was held in police custody until 30 July 1993. Between 16 July 1993 and 25 January 2000 the Istanbul State Security Court held thirty-six hearings. He died in July 2006 in a Turkish prison.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Court and the applicant’s inability to examine or have examined witnesses were. communicated to the Government. The application was declared inadmissible. The applicant was accused of trafficking illegal drugs in Turkey. He denied the charges and requested his acquittal. He was released pending trial in 2003. The application was dropped in 2008. The case was re-opened in 2009. The applicant was acquitted of all charges against him in 2010. He is currently living in the U.S. with his wife and two children. He has denied the allegations against him and has asked for his case to be dropped. The appeal has been rejected by the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic of Turkey. The original article stated that the applicant was charged with the trafficking of illegal drugs. We are happy to make clear that this was in fact not the case. The applicant was convicted of drug smuggling and sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment and a fine. He appealed the conviction, claiming that the evidence was insufficient to prove his involvement in the alleged acts. The Court of Cassation quashed the conviction in 2006. In July 2008 the İzmir Assize Court sentenced the applicant to twenty years and ten months of imprisonment. The higher court upheld the decision with a minor procedural correction in September 2009. The applicant has not returned to Turkey to challenge his conviction. The case is being heard by the Turkish Court of Appeal in Istanbul, which has the power to grant or deny a right of appeal to a Turkish citizen.

name: Jean-Claude Gacon
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1092/04) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the additional time granted to the Principal Public Prosecutor for appealing against a judgment of the Criminal Court amounted to a breach of the principle of equality of arms. On 16 October 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application. It also decided to examine the merits of this application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention) The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Saint-Didier-au-Mont-d’Or. The applicant and his brother were committed to stand trial in the Lyons Criminal Court. They were charged in particular with having deceived the social security scheme and the relevant health insurance offices through fraudulent practices. The Lyon Criminal Court held that the prosecution had lapsed as the offence of professional collusion was covered by an automatic amnesty, and that it lacked jurisdiction to examine the claims of the civil parties. The applicant was accordingly acquitted. The Principal Public Prosecutor lodged an appeal against the judgment on 20 April 2001, availing himself of the two-month time-limit granted to him for that purpose by Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that it was incompatible with the guarantees of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing that the time available to the Principal Public Prosecutor for lodging an appeal under Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was incompatible with Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. In a judgment of 25 June 2003 the Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal. The applicant was accordingly sentenced to a suspended term of two years’ imprisonment, ordered to pay a fine of 120,000 euros (EUR) and stripped of his civic, civil and family rights for five years. He was also ordered, jointly and severally with his brother, to pay the sum of EUR 442,573.13 in compensation.

name: Patrick Benjamin
train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that they had not had available to them a procedure by which they could challenge the lawfulness of their continued detention. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 23 October 1997 and transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court. The case was decided in favour of the applicants. The second applicant, Mr Hueth Wilson, was sentenced to life imprisonment for buggery of a young girl in 1977. The court had before it psychiatric evidence to the effect that he suffered from mental illness. Expert psychiatric evidence recommended that he should be made subject to a hospital order. Due to an absence of any beds in hospitals providing the level of security that the trial judge considered necessary, the judge felt unable to make the orders and passed, instead, a discretionary life sentence. His tariff period (the minimum period of detention satisfying the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at six years and expired in April 1989. His time in prison was characterised by periods of thought disorder, delusions and behavioural problems and the Secretary of State decided that he was in need of care and treatment. The applicants were not eligible for review by the discretionary lifer panels empowered by section 34 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 to order their release on licence. Leave to apply for judicial review of the decisions was granted on 17 May 1993. In June 1993, following consultation with the trial judge and the Lord Chief Justice, the Secretary of State decided that the second applicant should be regarded as a “technical lifer”. On 6 July 1996 the MHR Tribunal found that they were not satisfied that he no longer required treatment in hospital for mental illness. His case was reviewed most recently on 13 June 2000 when the Tribunal again did not recommend discharge.

name: Filiz Uyan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7496/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Ms Filiz Uyan (“the applicant’s” representative) had been convicted of being a member of a terrorist organisation and sentenced to twenty-two years’ imprisonment. The applicant was taken to a consultation room located on the ground floor. The bottom of the consulting room windows was only 50 cm above floor level and the windows were unprotected. The male security officers refused to leave the consultation room for security reasons. They stated that they would wait behind a folding screen. The proceedings against the male prison guard were dropped on 3 December 2001. The applicant’s lawyer filed a complaint against the doctor who had not asked the male security officers to leave the room. The doctor was issued with a warning for professional misconduct, namely for not taking the initiative to request the maleSecurity officers to left the consultation room or remove the applicant's handcuffs, as required by ethical rules. The Turkish Medical Association quashed that decision on 5 October 2002. The case was heard at the Karşıyaka Assize Court on 29 July 2002, and was settled out of court. The court ruled that the doctor had not treated the applicant disrespectfully.

The complaint concerned the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the military court, the alleged interference with the applicant's right to freedom of expression and the alleged. lack of an effective remedy to the Government. The applicant was represented by Ms A. J. Stock, Mr M. Muller, Mr T. Otty and Ms J. Gordon. name: Fabrice Gardel
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 16428/05) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, in particular, of his placement on the national register of sex offenders following his conviction. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of theApplication at the same time (Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention). The applicant was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment and stripped of all his civil, civic and family rights for ten years. Fabrice Gardel was convicted of sexual abuse of a minor under the age of 15 in 2003. He was sentenced to six years' imprisonment and a judicial and social supervision order. Gardel applied to have his sentence suspended on the grounds that his survival was not in doubt. The court also took into consideration medical reports according to which the applicant suffered from congenital heart disease which made any physical activity impossible. On 22 November 2005 the applicant was informed by a police officer from l’Haÿ-les-Roses police station that his name was being entered in the Sex Offenders Register on account of his conviction by the Meuse Assize Court, in accordance with the transitional provisions of the above‑mentioned Law. I acknowledge having been informed that: I have been finally convicted of an offence carrying a sentence of ten years or more. Accordingly, I am required to provide proof of my address by reporting in person every six months. ... I take note of the fact that if I leave the country my obligation to report in person will be suspended for the duration of my stay abroad but that I must continue to provide Proof of My Address by means of a registered letter with recorded delivery to the authority managing the Sex Offenders Register. I further acknowledge that I have the following rights: (i) under the Data Protection Act and Article 706-53-9, I may obtain a copy of all the information concerning me in the register. “I may apply to the public prosecutor at the Nantes tribunal de grande instance to have the information in the register rectified or deleted,” he said. “If the decision forming the basis for my placement on the register was issued by a foreign judicial authority, I may apply,’ he added, “‘to have the frequency of reporting reduced to once a year.’” “I can also apply. by applying to the. public prosecutor in whose district I am resident, in accordance with Articles R 53-8-27 et. seq.,” said the judge.

train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court ruled that Turkey had violated the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the THKP-C (Turkish People’s Liberation Party/Front). He was detained on remand and tried in the İstanbul Martial Law Court. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to lifetime imprisonment under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. In 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections and this case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. the Court declared the application admissible and the applicant was sentenced to life imprisonment. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the first instance court failed to establish the applicant's involvement in certain of the alleged crimes. Following promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993, which abolished the jurisdiction of the Martial Law Courts, the Court of Cassation (Yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case and on 4 January 1994 the case file was transmitted to it. The applicant appealed. the same day. On 18 April 1995 the Courtof Cassation upheld the applicant’s conviction and the case was retried. The case was adjourned until April 1997 when the applicant was found not guilty of any crime. The trial was concluded on April 15, 1998, and the applicant appealed again. The appeal was rejected and the application was dismissed.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11564/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a gynaecologist, was born in 1956 and lives in İzmir. He was arrested and taken into police custody at his medical practice. He alleges that, while he was in police custody, he was ill‑treated. He complains of having received electric shocks, of having been suffocated, and of being beaten and threatened. He also alleges that during the first three days of his detention, he had been deprived of food and medication and prevented from sleeping. The applicant was heard first by the public prosecutor and later by a judge at the İzmir State Security Court. The latter ordered his release from custody. The applicant did not object to this decision. The criminal proceedings brought against the applicant before the � Turkey State Security. Court for aiding and abetting an illegal armed organisation ended on 23 May 2000 with his acquittal. The application was dismissed on 26 November 1999. The decision was made because none of the persons put forward as witnesses by the applicant were able to confirm the applicant’s version of events, that the applicant was unable to identify the alleged perpetrators and that no medical reports noted any physical findings of ill-treatment.

name: Vincent Kelly
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30054/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants, next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Loughgall on 8 May 1987, alleged that their relatives had been kill unjustifiably. They invoked Articles 2, 6, 14 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Jordan v. the United UK ( no. 24746/94). The application was made by the. Human Rights Commission on 23 March 2000, which had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicants accepted that the summaries below are an accurate reflection of the written statements made by. the official personnel involved, without making any admission as to the credibility, consistency and veracity of these statements. The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Korff. The Chamber declared the application admissible. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights. The RUC station, which operated on a part-time basis only, was opened as normal at 9 a.m. on 8 May 1987. Three armed men who said they were from the IRA entered the house of the Mackle family in Aghinlig Upper, Dungannon. The men said they wanted to borrow the digger and one of the sons was brought outside to fill it with diesel. At about 6.30 p.m., a vehicle pulled up outside and a fourth man arrived. It appears that a bomb containing 300 to 400 pounds of explosives was prepared in the yard of the house and placed in the bucket of a digger. A blue Hiace van came from the Loughgall direction and parked outside the station. A man, dressed in blue overalls and wearing a balaclava, emerged from the rear of the van. He raised his rifle and began to shoot at the RUC station. Soldiers A to E, who had positioned themselves at windows on the first floor of the station began to return fire without warning. Soldier B received a facial injury from flying glass after a window by which he was standing was broken by gunfire. One of the IRA men drove the digger through the front gate and Soldier B, having spotted this, fired a short burst at the driver. The digger stopped and shortly afterwards there was an explosion. Soldiers A, B, D and E moved towards the front of the RUC station. Constables B and C were led outside by Constable A and Soldier C, who administered first aid to them. Soldier F also left the station by the rear and did not take any part in the shooting. Soldiers K and R observed what they thought was a gunman lying in the grass behind the police station. Both soldiers fired several rounds at what turned out to be a large lump of wood. Soldier V fired at a man in a blue boiler suit crossing the road in a crouched manner. Soldier K saw a man whom he apprehended, tied his hands and feet and handed him over to RUC who arrested him. The bodies of three soldiers were found lying in the driveway of the RUC station. The bodies were wearing blue boiler suits except where specified otherwise. The driver of the white Citroen car was dead at the wheel of the car. There were two significantly bullet damaged vehicles, a blue Toyota Hiace van with approximately 125 bullet holes in the bodywork. In the vicinity of the junction of Clovenden Road/Ballygasey Road there were bullet damaged Vauxhall Cavalier and Ford estate cars. The first body (Patrick Kelly) was found lying on his back still moving. Soldier X checking the body found that the man was holding a cigarette lighter. Police investigation of the incident began at 7.35pm. Post mortem examination revealed at least a dozen wounds to the torso and head. Discharge abrasion on an entry wound on the front of the neck indicated that when the gun was discharged the muzzle was within several feet of the body. There were four loaded rifles and one shotgun found in the van. Three of the stocks were folded. The sixth body (Eugene Kelly), which had massive head damage and multiple injuries elsewhere, was seated in the driver seat. There was a revolver lying between the driver’s seat and his door. The seventh body (Declan Arthurs) was lying in a lane-way opposite the premises of the Loughgall Football Club. The bodies of Antony Hughes and John McAlister were found in Loughgall, Northern Ireland on 9 May 1987. The ninth body (Antony Hughes) was seated with the seat belt on in the driver’s seat of the white Citroen car. The body was not wearing a boiler suit. The post mortem examination showed twenty-nine wounds (bullet and shrapnel). At 10.35 p.m. on 8 May 1987, the police took possession of the firearms used by Soldiers A to X which were delivered the following day to the Northern Ireland Forensic Science Laboratory for examination. In total, 678 spent cartridge cases were recovered, 78 of which were from IRA weapons. The inquest into the deaths of the three men was opened and adjourned on 30 May 1995. The hearing of the inquest proceeded without representation for any of the nine families. On the first day of the hearing the families asked for the. proceedings to be adjourned to allow them to seek judicial review of the decision to. refuse access to the witness statements. This step was taken on 31 May 1995 following consultation with the families and because it was felt “utterly impossible for the applicants’ interests to be fairly or adequately represented given the rulings of the Coroner’s office”. The inquest concluded on 8 September 1994. Inquest concluded on 2 June 1995 that all nine men had died from serious and multiple gun shot wounds. Justice McCollum in the High Court refused to quash the Coroner’s decisions or the jury verdict. In doing so, the judge placed considerable emphasis on the character of an inquest as a fact finding exercise and not a method of apportioning guilt. Seven of the families (the relatives of Antony Hughes, Kevin Antony McKearney, Michael Gormley, Seamus Donnelly, Declan Arthurs, Gerard O’Callaghan and Eugene Kelly) issued civil proceedings against the Ministry of Defence.

The soldiers were on full alert when, between 7.15 and 7.30 p.m., the blue van came from the Loughgall direction and parked outside the station on the far side of the road facing Armagh. A man, dressed in blue overalls and wearing a balaclava, emerged from the rear of the van and began to shoot at the R UC station. Soldiers A to E, who had positioned themselves at windows on the first floor of the station began to return fire without warning. Soldiers A, B, D and E moved towards the front of the RUC station and continued to fire at the men near the van. Constables B and C were led outside by Constable A and Soldier C, who administered first aid to them. Soldier F also left the station by the rear and did not take any part in the shooting. Soldier V fired at a man in a blue boiler suit crossing the road in a crouched manner. Soldier S passing the body saw no weapon near it. Soldiers S, T and U opened automatic fire on a white Citroen car. The front seat passenger got out of the car despite a warning from Soldier U not to move. Soldier X checking the body found that the man was holding a cigarette lighter. Other vehicles near the scene of the attack included a red Sierra 15 metres from position 6, occupied by a woman and her daughter, a blue Escort about 70 metres from the scene which was empty and a white Sierra, with three female occupants. These cars, or their occupants, were directed to positions of safety by soldiers as soon as the opportunity arose. The bodies were wearing blue boiler suits except where specified otherwise. The sixth body (Eugene Kelly), which had massive head damage and multiple injuries elsewhere, was seated in the driver seat. There was a revolver lying between the driver’s seat and his door. The seventh body (Declan Arthurs) was lying in a lane-way opposite the premises of the Loughgall Football Club. This body was not wearing a boiler suit and there was a cigarette lighter close to the right hand. The bodies were found in a white Citroen car in Loughgall, Northern Ireland. The ninth body (Antony Hughes) was seated with the seat belt on in the driver’s seat of the car. The post mortem examination showed twenty-nine wounds (bullet and shrapnel). Spent cartridge cases were recovered from all over the crime scene which stretched from the junction of Cloveneden Road/Ballygasey Road to the Church/Church Hall. The RUC forwarded a report to the Director of Public Prosecutions for Northern Ireland (the DPP) on the outcome of their RUC investigation. On 22 September 1988, he concluded that the evidence did not warrant the prosecution of any person involved in the shootings. The inquest into the deaths of the men in the present case was opened on 30 May 1995 in public before a Coroner and a jury of 10 members. The hearing of the inquest proceeded without representation for any of the nine families. The Coroner made available the maps and photographs but did not permit counsel (other than those instructed on the Coroner’s behalf) to see witness statements until the witness was giving evidence. This step was taken on 31 May 1995 following consultation with the families and because it was felt “utterly impossible for the applicants’ interests to be fairly or adequately represented given the rulings”. The inquest concluded that all nine men died from serious and multiple gun shot wounds. None of the soldiers appeared but their statements were lodged. The family of Declan Arthurs sought judicial review of the Coroner’s decisions not to allow the legal representatives to see witness statements before they gave evidence. In his judgment of 24 May 1996, Mr Justice McCollum in the High Court refused to quash the Cor coroner's decisions or the jury verdict. In doing so, the judge placed considerable emphasis on the character of an inquest as a fact finding exercise and not a method of apportioning guilt. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30054/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants were next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Loughgall on 8 May 1987. They alleged that their relatives had been kill unjustifiably, without any attempt being made to bring them before a court. They invoked Articles 2, 6, 14 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Jordan v. the United UK ( no. 24746/94). The application was brought by the. Human Rights Commission on 23 March 2000, which had been given leave by. the President to intervene in the written procedure. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Korff. The applicants accepted that the summaries below are an accurate reflection of the written statements made by the official personnel involved, without making any admission as to the credibility, consistency and veracity of these statements. The application was declared admissible by the Chamber of the Court of Appeal. The RUC station, which operated on a part-time basis only, was opened as normal at 9 a.m. on 8 May 1987. Soldiers O, P, Q and R were instructed to position themselves in a wooded area to the south of the Loughgall Road, near what is known as Ballygasey Cottage. Three armed men who said they were from the IRA entered the house of the Mackle family in Aghinlig Upper, Dungannon. The men said they wanted to borrow the digger and one of the sons was brought outside to fill it with diesel. At about 6.30 p.m., a vehicle pulled up outside and a fourth man arrived. It appears that a bomb containing 300 to 400 pounds of explosives was prepared in the yard. The incident at Loughgall took place between 7.15 and 7.30 p.m. The soldiers reported a number of sightings of the blue Hiace van passing in front of the RUC station in both directions. Reports that the van had been hijacked, and that a digger was acting suspiciously in the area, were also received. Given this information and the knowledge that diggers had been used in previous terrorist attacks, the soldiers were on full alert when the incident occurred. The remaining two gunmen left the house at about 7.10 p. m. The family's phone and neighbour's phone were out of order but two of the sons eventually alerted a police patrol. Soldiers A, B, D and E continued to fire at the men near the van. Constables B and C were led outside by Constable A and Soldier C. Soldier F also left the station by the rear and did not take any part in the shooting. Soldiers K and R observed what they thought was a gunman lying in the grass behind the police station. He failed to stand up when challenged to do so, and both soldiers fired several rounds at what turned out to be a large lump of wood. Soldier K saw a man whom he apprehended, tied his hands and feet and handed him over to the RUC who arrested him. This man was a Mr Tennyson who was not involved in the attack. When the soldiers. arrived at the RUC station, there had been a white Citroen car right behind them. After shooting started but before the bomb went off, this car began to reverse towards the soldiers in position 5. Soldiers S, T and U opened automatic fire on the car and when they stopped firing the vehicle was about 20 metres away. The front seat passenger got out of the car despite a warning from Soldier U not to move. Almost immediately, he was hit by gunfire and he fell to the ground. Later realising that he was still alive, Soldiers S and U moved him onto the pavement and put two field dressings on his wounds. Soldier X checking the body found that the man was holding a cigarette lighter. The pathologist observed at least twenty separate missile wounds (i.e. bullet and fragment) and found that discharge abrasion on an entry wound on the front of the neck indicated that when the gun was discharged the muzzle was within several feet of the body. There were four loaded rifles and one shotgun found in the van. The post mortem examination revealed at least a dozen wounds to the torso and head. The eighth body (Gerald O’Callaghan) was lying on its right side on the pavement at the Loughgall side of the lane-way. The seventh body (Declan Arthurs) was not wearing a boiler suit and there was a cigarette lighter close to the right hand. The ninth body (Antony Hughes) was seated with the seat belt on in the driver’s seat of the white Citroen car. The body was not wearing a boiler suit. The post mortem examination showed twenty-nine wounds (bullet and shrapnel). At 10.35 p.m. on 8 May 1987, the police took possession of the firearms used by Soldiers A to X which were delivered the following day to the Northern Ireland Forensic Science Laboratory for examination. In total, 678 spent cartridge cases were recovered, 78 of which were from IRA weapons. The RUC forwarded a report to the Director of Public Prosecutions for Northern Ireland (the DPP) on the outcome of their RUC investigation. The inquest into the deaths of the three men was opened and adjourned on 30 May 1995. The hearing was adjourned after the families of the victims asked for access to witness statements. The families were refused and the inquest was called off. The inquest was re-opened on 8 September 1994 with a jury of 10 members. The jury was told by the Coroner that there were no further witnesses to be heard. The Court of Appeal ruled that the families could not be represented at the inquest. The case was then referred to the High Court for further proceedings. The High Court ruled in March 1994 that the inquest should be reopened and the families allowed access to the statements. Family of Declan Arthurs sought judicial review of the Coroner’s decisions not to allow the legal representatives to see witness statements before they gave evidence. None of the soldiers appeared but their statements were lodged. It was concluded on 2 June 1995 that all nine men had died from serious and multiple gun shot wounds. In his judgment of 24 May 1996, Mr Justice McCollum in the High Court refused to quash the Cor coroner's decisions or the jury verdict. In doing so, the judge placed considerable emphasis on the character of an inquest as a fact finding exercise and not a method of apportioning guilt.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24820/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1960 and is currently serving a prison sentence in Edirne. The application was declared partly inadmissible and the complaints concerning the lack of legal assistance during the applicant’s police custody and his inability to question some of the witnesses were communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The case was decided in favour of the applicant on 18 January 2011. The applicant was convicted of being a member of an illegal organisation. He was sentenced to twelve years and six months in prison. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicant's appeal in 2005. The court relied on the statements of the co-accused, and also took into consideration other items of evidence. The case against the applicant has been referred to as the 'TDP' case. The TDP is a terrorist organisation based in the Turkish city of Erzurum. It was founded in 1999 and claimed to have more than 3,000 members. It has been linked to the death of a local police officer in 2000.

The purpose of the request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 1, 8 and 13 (art. 6-1, art. 8, 13) of the Convention. The five judges thus designated were Mr. J. Cremona, Mr. W. Ganshof van der Meersch,. Mr. D. Evrigenis and Mr. G. Lagergren. The Government filed their memorial on 28 November. On 27 January 1978, a memorial by the Principal Delegate of the Commission was received at the registry. At a meeting held in private on 18 November in Strasbourg, the Chamber decided under Rule 48 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The Court held a preparatory meeting on 10 March, immediately before the opening of the hearings. At that meeting the Court, granting a request presented by the Government, decided that their Agent and counsel would be authorised to address the Court in German. The Government undertaking, inter alia, responsibility for the interpretation into French or English of their oral arguments or statements. The applicants, who are German nationals, are Gerhard Klass, an Oberstaatsanwalt, Peter Lubberger, a lawyer, Jürgen Nussbruch, a judge, Hans-Jürgen Pohl and Dieter Selb, lawyers. All five applicants claim that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) and a statute enacted in pursuance of that provision are contrary to the Convention. They do not dispute that the State has the right to have recourse to the surveillance measures contemplated by the legislation. They challenge this legislation in that it permits those measures without obliging the authorities in every case to notify the persons concerned after the event. The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany were prompted by this judgment to propose amendments to the G 10, but the parliamentary proceedings have not yet been completed. Although, as a precautionary measure, the applicants claimed before both the Constitutional Court and the Commission that they were being subjected to surveillance measures, they did not know whether they had actually been applied to them. At no time have surveillance measures provided for by the Act enacted in pursuance of Article 10 of the Basic Law been ordered or implemented against the applicants. Neither as persons suspected of one or more of the offences specified in the Act nor as third parties within the meaning of Article 1, paragraph 2, sub-paragraph 2, have the applicants been subjected to such measures. No question of the applicants’ having been indirectly involved in a surveillance measure directed against another person. After the end of the Second World War, the surveillance of mail, post and telecommunications in Germany was dealt with by the occupying powers. The Government wished to substitute the domestic law for the rights exercised by the Three Powers and to place under legal control interferences with the right, guaranteed by Article 10 of the Basic Law, to respect for correspondence. The two Acts, having been adopted by the federal legislative assemblies, were enacted on 24 June and 13 August 1968 respectively. in such cases the person concerned is notified of the surveillance measure.“ The contested legislation was introduced on 13 June 1967, the Government introduced two Bills as part of the Emergency Legislation. The first sought primarily to amend Article 10 para. 2 of the basic law; the second was designed to limit the right to secrecy. The Act of 24 June 1968 provides for secrecy of mail, post and telecommunications. Restrictions may be ordered only pursuant to a statute, says the G 10. Such restrictions are intended to protect the ‘free democratic constitutional order’ and the security of the (allied) armed forces stationed on the territory of the Republic. The surveillance may cover only ‘the suspect or such other persons who are, on the basis of the factual indications, suspected of planning, committing or having committed certain criminal acts punishable under the Criminal Code’ says the Article 1 para. 1 of the Act. The G 10, adopting the solution contemplated by the second sentence of paragraph 2 of the above-quoted Article 10, specifies the cases in which the competent authorities may impose restrictions. The measures are ordered, on written application giving reasons, either by the supreme Land authority in cases falling within its jurisdiction or by a Federal Minister empowered for the purpose by the Chancellor. Measures ordered must be immediately discontinued once the required conditions have ceased to exist or the measures themselves are no longer necessary. Measures remain in force for a maximum of three months and may be renewed only on fresh application. Under the terms of Article 1 para. 5, sub-paragraph 5, the person concerned is not to be notified of the restrictions affecting him. However, since the Federal Constitutional Court’s judgment of 15 December 1970 (see paragraph 11 above), the competent authority has to inform the person. concerned as soon as notification can be made. The G 10 Commission decides, ex officio or on application by a person believing himself to be under surveillance, on both the legality of and the necessity for the measures. The Commission draws up its own rules of procedure which must be approved by the Board. Before taking this decision, the Board consults the Government. For the Länder, their legislatures lay down the parliamentary supervision. to which the supreme authorities are supreme. The G 10 commission is independent in the exercise of its functions and cannot be subject to instructions. In practice and except in urgent cases, the Minister seeks the prior consent of this Commission. The Government, moreover, intend proposing to Parliament to make such prior consent obligatory. According to Article 1 para. 9, sub-paragraph 5, of the G 10: “... there shall be no legal remedy before the courts in respect of the ordering and implementation of restrictive measures.” The surveillance of the post and telecommunications of a certain person can serve a useful purpose only if the person concerned does not become aware of it. The Bill presented during the 4th legislative session ... provided for the ordering (of such measures) by an independent judge. The Federal Government abandoned this solution in the Bill amending Article 10 of the Basic Law, introduced as part of the Emergency Legislation, mainly because the Executive should retain the responsibility for such decisions in order to observe a clear separation of powers. The Commission on 11/11 lodged its application to the European Court of Human Rights with the European Commission. The application was denied on the grounds that there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the complaint. The European Commission is now considering the case and will make a decision on it in the next few weeks. The Commission has decided that the application should be allowed to go ahead and is seeking a ruling on the matter within the next two months. The case is expected to be heard by the Commission on the 11/12/2014. It will be heard at a hearing on the 12/11/2014, which will be attended by the European Commissioner for Human Rights, Joerg Forbrig and the European Parliament’s Justice Committee. The applicants alleged that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the G 10 violate Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. On 18 December 1974, the Commission declared the application admissible. Some of the applicants are barristers and it is theoretically excluded that they are in fact subject to secret surveillance in consequence of contacts they may have with clients who are suspected of anti-constitutional activities. The Commission then expressed the opinion:by eleven votes to one with two abstentions, that the present case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) The applicants relied on the notion “civil rights’;.  case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) in so far as the applicants relied on the notion “criminal charge’ Delegates of the Commission made the following concluding submissions to the Court: “Whether, having regard to the circumstances of the case, the applicants could claim to be ‘victims’ of a violation of their rights guaranteed by the Convention by reason of the system of surveillance established by the so-called G 10 Act’” The report contains various separate opinions on whether the applicants are actually victims of a violated rights set forth in the Convention.
