name: Gerard Magee
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28135/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged he was ill-treated while in detention and that he was denied a fair trial. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The applicant was interviewed five times by two teams of two detectives. During the sixth interview the applicant broke his silence and gave detailed answers to a number of questions. The applicant was medically examined that evening at 8.20 p.m. The doctor gave the applicant two tablets (a mild analgesic) and prescribed four such tablets a day if required. At 1 p.M. the applicant was allowed to consult with his solicitor, who made notes on the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. The solicitor chose not to pass these complaints on to the police. The Applicant was interviewed about another matter between 10 a.m and 12.45 p. m. on 18 December 1988. He was then interviewed for the last time about an unrelated matter. The applicant, along with others, was charged at Belfast Magistrates' Court with conspiracy to cause explosions, possession of explosives with intent, conspiracy to murder and membership of the Irish Republican Army. The prosecution case was based on the admissions made by the applicant in interview and, in particular, the written statements signed by him. The trial of the applicant and his co-accused began at Belfast Crown Court before a single judge sitting without a jury. The applicant did not subsequently give evidence at the trial. However, the trial judge cautioned the applicant for breaching the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (as amended) He applied to have the admissions and statement made during questioning excluded on the basis of his alleged ill-treatment. The judge rejected the application. The trial judge summarised the applicant's evidence of ill-treatment and this summary was later accepted on appeal by the applicant as constituting an accurate account of his evidence in this respect. On the question of general credibility the judge found that the applicant had repeatedly lied to the court, whereas the detectives involved were not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination. As to the ESDA evidence, the trial judge found it impossible to accept that ill- treatment could have gone on without it being picked up by the cameras in the room where the applicant was questioned. The applicant was sentenced to 18 months in prison, suspended for 12 months, and fined £500. The trial judge rejected the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. On 11 January 1991 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment. The applicant's appeal against conviction was heard by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland. The court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. Accordingly, on 16 June 1993 the applicant’s appeal was rejected. On 17 December 1993 the appeal against his sentence was rejected, and he was jailed for 20 years. The case was settled at Belfast Crown Court in January 1992. The trial judge ruled in favour of the applicant and sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

The case originated in an application (no. 28135/95) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that he was ill-treated while in detention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The decision was made in favor of the applicant and the Government of the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland. The applicant complained to the same doctor he had seen the day before of ill-treatment during the second and third interviews on the previous day. The doctor gave the applicant two tablets (a mild analgesic) and prescribed four such tablets a day if required. At 1 p.m. the applicant was allowed to consult with his solicitor, who made notes on the applicant's allegations. The solicitor chose not to pass these complaints on to the police. During the sixth interview the applicant broke his silence and gave detailed answers to a number of questions admitting to his involvement in the assembly and planting of the bomb. The applicant was medically examined that evening at 8.20pm. The applicant was charged with conspiracy to cause explosions, possession of explosives with intent, conspiracy to murder and membership of the Irish Republican Army. The trial of the applicant and his co-accused began at Belfast Crown Court before a single judge sitting without a jury. The prosecution case was based on the admissions made by the applicant in interview and, in particular, the written statements signed by him. The applicant applied under section 8 of the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (as amended) to have the admissions and statement made during questioning excluded on the basis of his alleged ill-treatment. A voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury) began and the applicant gave evidence as to his treatment by one team of two detectives during interviews nos. 2, 4 and 6 while in Castlereagh police station. On 21 December 1990 the trial judge gave judgment. The only evidence against the applicant was the admissions and statement made while in custody at Castlereagh police station. The trial judge summarised the applicant's evidence of ill-treatment and this summary was later accepted on appeal by the applicant as constituting an accurate account of his evidence in this respect. On the question of general credibility the judge found that the applicant had repeatedly lied to the court, whereas the detectives involved were not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination in their firm denials. As to the ESDA evidence, the court found that it was consistent with the evidence presented in relation to others charged with offences arising out of the same incident. The trial judge rejected the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. On 11 January 1991 the applicant was sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment. The applicant's appeal against conviction was heard by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland in 1993. The court concluded that it was satisfied that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. The appeal was rejected on 16 June 1993. On 17 December 1993 the applicant’s appeal against his sentence was rejected. The appeals court noted that the trial judge had had the great advantage of seeing the applicant give evidence. It noted, inter alia, that both an accused and the police officers involved can equally have an incentive to lie.

name: Sarah Boyle
train_texts: The case was brought before the Court on 18 July 1986 by the European Commission of Human Rights. The case originated in two applications lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The purpose of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8 and 13. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir Vincent Evans, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The Government and the Delegate of the Commission had not wished to present any comments in writing. The President directed that the oral proceedings should open on 18 May 1987. The hearing was held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by the Government, by Sir Basil Hall for the Commission and by Mr. Lester for the applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. There appeared before the Court:. Mr. M. Wood, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent;. Mr M. Baker, Barrister-at-Law, Mr. A. Grotrian, Advocate, Counsel, Mrs M. Macdonald, Scottish Office; and. Mr D. Dalgetty, Scotland Office, Adviser. James and Sarah Boyle are British citizens born in 1944 and 1950 respectively. In 1967, the first applicant was sentenced in Scotland to life imprisonment for murder. He received a number of subsequent prison sentences in 1968 and 1973 for prison breaking, attempted murder of a prison officer and assault on prison staff. In March 1973, Mr. Boyle was removed from Peterhead Prison to a Special Unit in Barlinnie Prison. This Unit had been set up on an experimental basis to treat selected long-term prisoners and prisoners with violent propensities. The Unit had a maximum of eight prisoners and was characterised by a more liberal regime. Mr Boyle played a prominent role in facilitating the success of the Special Unit. Mr. Boyle chose Saughton Prison over Penninghame Open Prison on the basis that it would be more beneficial to him during the period leading to his eventual release. The factors governing the choice included the desirability of his occupying a single cell rather than being in a dormitory. Mr. Boyle himself had in fact stated in written submissions in December 1979 that, if he could not remain at Barlinnie for his pre-release programme, he would prefer training from Edinburgh. In November 1981, he was transferred to a Training for Freedom Hostel within the prison (see paragraph 33 below). He was released on 1 November 1982. As from October 1980 until his release, hewas in the lowest security category (Category D) Mr. Boyle was entitled to receive visits in accordance with the normal rules applied in Saughton Prison (see paragraph 26 below) As from November 1980, he was given a special licence to do unescorted community work outside the prison, initially for two days and subsequently for five days a week. He was able to benefit from the special escorted leave scheme and visited his home on two occasions, albeit under the constant supervision of an officer. He used this time to meet his wife, with the result that he was not able to see the other members of his family. Mr. Boyle also complained through his Member of Parliament to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration (the Ombudsman - see paragraph 39 below) Brian Rice was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder in 1967. He served his sentence in Peterhead and Perth Prisons until August 1979. From August 1979 onwards, he was detained as a Category D prisoner at Saughton Prison. He was moved to the Training for Freedom Hostel within the prison on 11 September 1981 and was released on licence on 1 June 1982. Brian Rice enjoyed the normal entitlement to visits applicable at the prison. He petitioned the Secretary of State for Scotland on 8 May 1981 requesting a home visit to his father. The decision recommended him to make the effort to get a member of staff to take him out of prison under the special escorted leave scheme. Brian Rice was not able to visit his father during the relevant period. He was permitted to attend, without an escort, a college to follow an educational course two days a week and also a centre where he was doing community work. He had previously been granted a home visit in August 1980 and prior to the commencement of the Training for Freedom programme he spent five days on home leave in September 1981. Mr. Rice was advised that if his father’s condition deteriorated he should make a further request. The reply of 2 September 1981 sent on behalf of the Secretary of State rejected all the various complaints raised. In particular, it was pointed out that all his mail had been posted.
